questions.question: When are two events independent?
choices: They can never occur together
They have equal probabilities
Knowing one occurred does not change the probability of the other
Their probabilities add to 1

questions.question: When are two events dependent?
choices: They must occur at the same time
Knowing one occurred changes the probability of the other
They must have different names
They each have probability 1/2

questions.question: Which formula applies to independent events A and B?
choices: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A) − P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A)/P(B)

questions.question: What is P(A given B) when A and B are independent and P(B) > 0?
choices: P(B)
P(A)

questions.question: Which experiment normally makes successive color draws independent?
choices: Drawing without replacement
Removing every ball of the first color drawn
Drawing from a mixed bag with replacement and remixing
Drawing only after changing the bag's contents

questions.question: A fair coin and fair six-sided die are used independently. What is the probability of heads and a 6?

choices: The events are independent
The events are mutually exclusive
The events have no common outcomes
The events are complementary

questions.question: Why are successive draws without replacement usually dependent?
choices: The first draw changes the names of the colors
The total number of original outcomes is infinite
Both draws must produce the same color
The first draw changes the contents for the second draw

Why are two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities not independent?
choices: The occurrence of one makes the other's probability zero
They always occur together
Their probabilities must both be 1/2
Their combined probability must exceed 1

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.3 and P(A given B) = 0.6, with P(B) > 0, what follows?
choices: A and B are independent
A and B are mutually exclusive
A and B must have equal probabilities
A and B are dependent

choices: P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B given A)
P(A and B) = P(A)P(B given A)
P(A and B) = P(B given A) − P(A)

questions.question: Does equal probability by itself prove two events independent?
choices: No; independence concerns whether one changes the other's probability
Yes; every pair with equal probabilities is independent
Yes; equal probabilities imply mutual exclusivity
No; independent events must have unequal probabilities
